summary: Qualitative reading of LLM oligopoly market transcripts, with independent GPT verification of each claim
logs: Qwen3-14B: only the 36 human-comparable markets are complete (NT-T n=2,4,6,8; T-NT and NT-NT n=4); the T-NT large-n group is skipped and other groups cover only the cells that exist.

result.summary: I read all 12 qwen3-14b NT-T markets at n=2 and n=4 (6 per cell). Chat in Part 2 almost never got prices back near 100. Firms agreed on a price close to their last Part-1 price and then held it with nearly perfect compliance for all 24 Talk periods. Only 1 of 12 markets (n2 m5) climbed step by step to 100, and only n4 m1 jumped from 1 to 50. This is the main gap with humans: the mean Talk selling price was 61.9 vs 93.5 for humans at n=2 and 13.2 vs 81.3 at n=4, and 0% of n=4 Talk periods sold at 100 vs 74.6% for humans. The firms are not misreading the game. Every probe answer in all 12 markets gives best_common_price = 100, yet firms keep a low agreed price, so the low prices look like a status-quo or risk-aversion choice rather than a misunderstanding. Agreements were rarely broken. The exception is n2 m0, where chat itself became a running list of announced undercuts that drove the price from 71 to 4. Threats ("if any deviate, all drop to 1") were common but were never carried out after a real deviation.

result.summary: Note first that this group has no n=10 data: there are 12 NT-T markets for qwen3-14b, 6 at n=6 and 6 at n=8. In Part 1 (no chat), prices fell to about 0–1 by period 6, which roughly matches the humans: selling price 0.875 vs 2.5 at n=6, and 0.72 vs 1.1 at n=8. Chat did not bring collusion. The mean Talk selling price was 2.67 at n=6 (humans 65.0) and exactly 1.0 at n=8 (humans 55.2). Firms coordinated easily and almost unanimously in chat, but mostly on keeping the competitive price of 1. Proposals of 50 or 100 were made in period 2.1 and voted down within one or two periods by an explicit 'no move without full consensus' norm. Every one of the 84 post-game probe answers gave 100 as the best common price, so the low prices are not a misread of the rules. Agreements were kept in 232 of 238 periods, but that mostly means firms kept to 1. All 6 broken agreements were firms that stayed at 1 while others raised. None was a covert undercut, and no firm posted 0 in Part 2. Chat at large n is formulaic: 69% of messages repeat verbatim a message the same firm sent earlier. Firms often get profits wrong and sometimes misread the rules. Most messages flagged as threats are warnings about risk, or 'we all drop to 1' threats made while every firm is already at 1.

result.summary: Only n=4 exists for this group. All six n=2 T-NT markets are *.failed.json/ckpt with no completed run (e.g. m0 was cancelled after 16 periods), so nothing here covers n=2. In all 6 n=4 T-NT markets, qwen3-14b colluded openly in chat from period 1.1 ("Let's collude to set the price at 70"). Every market settled on 70 or 75, never on 100, even though someone proposed 100 in 5 of the 6 markets and every firm's post-game probe answered best_common_price=100 in all six. Talk-phase prices (Part 1 from period 6: 61.7) are well below the human 89.0, but high prices carry over strongly once chat is removed (Part 2: 54.1 vs human 67.0, against 0.9 in the model's own NT-NT n=4 markets). In 4 of 6 markets the Part 2 price was at or near the last Part 1 price for at least 19 periods. Where prices fell, the fall was a 1-ECU lockstep ladder rather than a collapse. In 2 markets that ladder ran through chat itself: one firm announced or carried out a 1-ECU undercut and the others publicly agreed to match it, so talking drove prices down. In 2 other markets it began in Part 2 because a firm reasoned that no chat meant no enforcement, or misread the die rule.

result.summary: Qwen3-14B firms understand the rules. Every firm in every Talk market answers 100 as the best common price on the probe. Their recall of recent prices and die rolls is accurate (160 of 160 dated price recalls, 83 of 83 die-value mentions), and explicit profit arithmetic is mostly right. What sets them apart from humans is deliberate caution and status-quo anchoring, not misreading. Chat almost never moves prices toward 100. Firms agree on roughly the price they were already at (1–2 when n≥4; 25/50/80/95 when n=2; 70/75 when Talk comes first) and then keep that agreement almost perfectly, so 'kept agreement' rates of about 96–99% are kept low-price agreements. In 2 markets chat became a channel for announcing undercuts, and Talk prices fell well below NoTalk. Real mistakes exist but are a minority. About 5% of zero-price notes claim that price 0 earns 300 ECU, and a few profit numbers are wrong. Most zero prices (313 of 379) are knowingly chosen while acknowledging they earn nothing. Several rule-based chat codes (breach/deception at n=8, 'breaches' during lockstep declines) are coder artifacts, not real cheating. Real chat-versus-notes deception is concentrated in 2 markets.
